opus-5.5.text:
I think the big open question is really how you make the transition between the two without throwing away what you learned in pretraining. Imitation learning is great at getting you a policy that's in the right ballpark. You get natural-looking motions and reasonable behaviors, and you avoid a lot of the reward-engineering pain we've had in RL for locomotion. But once you start fine-tuning with RL, the policy can drift pretty quickly. It finds ways to exploit the reward, and you lose the nice properties that came from the demonstrations.

So there's a balance to strike. How much do you regularize toward the pretrained behavior, and how much freedom do you give RL to actually improve and become robust? Robustness is the thing RL is really good at. In simulation you can throw millions of perturbations at the robot, and that's something you just can't get from demonstrations alone.

There's also a practical side. A lot of the large pretrained models, especially the transformer-based or diffusion-style policies, are big and slow compared to the small MLPs we've traditionally trained with PPO in massively parallel simulation. Fine-tuning those big models with on-policy RL at the scale we're used to is not straightforward. You run into compute limits, stability issues, and questions about which parts of the network you should even update.

And then there's the data question. What distribution of demonstrations sets RL up best? Is it better to have broad, diverse but noisy data, or narrow, high-quality data? I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet. My sense is that the field is converging on this recipe of pretraining on lots of data and then fine-tuning with RL for robustness and precision. It's similar to what we've seen in language models. But the details of how to do it well for physical systems are still very much open.

r001.rationale: The response mentions using simulation for RL perturbations, but does not identify as an open question whether RL fine-tuning requires introducing a simulator when pretraining was done without one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good one to start with, because I think it's where a lot of the field is converging right now, and honestly I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet.

So the appeal is obvious. You pretrain a policy on demonstrations, whether that's motion capture, teleoperation, or data from some other controller, and you get a policy that already does something reasonable. Then you fine-tune it with RL so it can go beyond the demonstrations, handle contacts and perturbations the demonstrator never showed you, and actually be robust on the real robot. In principle you get the best of both.

The open question for me is what happens to the prior during fine-tuning. The moment you turn on RL with a task reward, the optimizer has no particular loyalty to the behavior you pretrained. If the reward is even slightly misaligned with the demonstrations, the policy will happily drift away, and you end up with the same jittery, weird-looking gaits you would have gotten training from scratch, just reached a bit faster. So you add a regularizer, a KL penalty toward the initial policy, or an adversarial motion prior, or you keep mixing demonstration data in. But then you've introduced a knob that trades off style against task performance, and nobody really knows how to set that knob in a principled way. Too strong and the policy can't fix the mistakes in the demonstrations. Too weak and it forgets them.

The second piece is distribution shift in the other direction. Demonstrations live on a narrow manifold of states. RL immediately pushes the policy off that manifold, and the pretrained features may be completely uninformative there. So you're asking: is the pretraining giving you good representations, or just a good initial action distribution? My suspicion is that for a lot of locomotion work it's mostly the second thing, and that's why the benefits sometimes look smaller than people expect.

And then there's the practical question of scale. With legged robots we've been very successful training from scratch in simulation because simulation is cheap and reward design is tractable. For humanoids doing whole-body manipulation, reward design gets really painful, and that's exactly where demonstrations should help the most. So the interesting question isn't really whether to combine them. It's at what point, on what kind of task, the demonstrations start carrying information that you genuinely can't recover from reward alone, and how you keep that information alive through fine-tuning without freezing the policy in place.

astra-6.text: I think the open question is how to combine the strengths of the two. With imitation learning, you can get a policy that does something useful, but then how do you fine-tune it with reinforcement learning without losing what you learned from the demonstrations? You want it to improve beyond the data, while preserving the behaviors that were already good. And how much demonstration data do you actually need to give reinforcement learning a good starting point? I think that balance is still an open question.

sol-6.1.text: I think the open question is how to combine the strengths of both. With imitation learning, you can use demonstrations to get a good initial behavior, and then reinforcement learning can potentially improve on that. But how do you make that transition without losing what you learned during pretraining? And can reinforcement learning reliably take you beyond the demonstrations, rather than just recover a similar behavior? Understanding what makes that combination work consistently is, I think, still a very interesting research question.
